transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess what brought me in is I keep checking things over and over—boxes, lists, drawers in the condo—before I can move on. I know I’ve already looked, but I still feel like I have to check again. My wife will be waiting for me to just leave it alone, and I can’t seem to do that right away.
When you feel the need to check things again, do you have upsetting thoughts or mental images that come to mind, like a fear something bad will happen if you don’t check?

Yes, it’s more like a nagging thought than a picture. I’ll think, “What if I threw away something important from my old teaching files?” or “What if I put a tool I’m going to need in the wrong box?” I can tell myself it’s probably fine, but the thought comes back anyway, and then I have trouble settling down until I check.
Do you feel you have to perform certain actions a specific number of times or in a certain way to prevent something bad from happening, even if it seems unnecessary?

Not really a number, no. It’s more that I have to check in a certain way, I guess—look through the same boxes, go back over the list, open the condo drawers again—before I feel like I can move on. I know I already looked, but I still end up doing it again, even when my wife is waiting and I know I should just leave it alone.
Does this checking behavior cause you significant distress or interfere with your daily activities, such as being late or not being able to focus on other things?

Yes, it does interfere. It’s not ruining my whole day, but unpacking the condo has taken a lot longer than it should because I keep stopping to verify things. And I’ve been putting off getting ready for my library tutoring and some hobbies, because I feel like I can’t really move on until I’m sure everything is checked enough.
Do these nagging thoughts ever feel intrusive or unwanted, and do you try to resist them, or do they feel more like normal worries that you just can’t let go of easily?

They feel intrusive, yes. I don’t really want to be thinking about it. I’ll tell myself, “You probably didn’t throw anything important away,” or “That tool is probably in the right box,” but then the thought comes back anyway. It’s not like a normal worry I can just set aside easily—it keeps nagging at me until I check.
Besides checking things repeatedly, do you find yourself doing any other behaviors or mental acts to try to reduce the anxiety or discomfort that comes with these nagging thoughts?

Mostly it’s the checking. I keep going back to the same boxes, the lists, and the condo drawers before I feel like I can move on. I know I already looked, and I know my wife is waiting for me to just leave it alone, but I still feel like I have to look again to settle myself.

Do you feel driven to perform these checking behaviors in response to your nagging thoughts, almost like a way to neutralize the anxiety they bring, even though you know they might not make much sense?

Yes, that’s pretty much it. I feel like I have to check the same boxes, the lists, or the condo drawers again before I can move on. I know I already looked, and it doesn’t really make sense to keep doing it, but the nagging feeling doesn’t settle until I go back and check. My wife is waiting for me to just leave it alone, and I wish I could, but I get pulled back into it.
Do these checking behaviors and nagging thoughts take up more than an hour of your day?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t timed it. Some days it feels like it adds up, but I couldn’t honestly say whether it’s more than an hour.

Do these nagging thoughts and the need to check things feel different from regular worries, like they come into your mind uncontrollably and are completely separate from actual concerns you have, or do they feel more like everyday worries that are just harder to let go of?

They feel more like they just pop back in, not like a normal worry I can reason through and be done with. I’ll think maybe I threw away something important from my old teaching files, or maybe I put a tool in the wrong box. Even when I tell myself that’s probably not true, the thought comes back and I can’t really settle until I check.
When you’re checking the boxes, lists, or drawers again, are you trying to prevent something bad from happening, like making a mistake or losing something important, even if you know it’s unlikely?

Yes, I think that’s part of it. I’m checking because I’m afraid I’ll miss something or leave something important in the wrong place, even though I know I already looked. With the boxes, the lists, the condo drawers—I keep going back over them before I can move on. My wife is usually waiting for me to just stop, and I know she’s right, but it’s hard to leave it alone.

Besides checking things again, do you ever feel the need to think certain thoughts, repeat words silently, or do anything else in your mind to reduce the anxiety that comes with these nagging thoughts?

Not really like repeating words or saying things in my head, no. It’s more the checking itself. I get stuck going back to the same boxes, the lists, the condo drawers, even though I know I already looked. I just have trouble moving on until I check again, and my wife is usually waiting for me to leave it alone.
Can you estimate how much time you spend each day going back to check the boxes, lists, or condo drawers? Does it add up to more than an hour in total?

I’m not sure exactly how much time it adds up to. It can be a fair bit, because I keep going back to the same boxes or lists or drawers before I can move on. I know I already looked, and my wife is often waiting for me to just leave it be, but I still feel like I need to check again.
Do you find it hard to throw things away or feel the need to save items, even if they don’t seem useful to others?
I don’t think so, no. I haven’t really noticed a problem with saving things or not being able to throw things away. That’s not something that stands out to me.
Do you ever experience sudden, repetitive movements or sounds that you can’t control, like blinking repeatedly, shrugging your shoulders, or making noises without meaning to?
No, I don’t think so. I haven’t noticed anything like repeated movements or sounds I can’t control.
Do these nagging thoughts or checking behaviors cause you noticeable emotional distress, such as anxiety, frustration, or guilt, even when you know they might not make sense?

Yes, it does bother me. It’s not usually overwhelming, but I get these nagging thoughts that maybe I threw away something important from my old teaching files, or put a tool in the wrong box. I’ll tell myself it probably doesn’t matter or it’s unlikely, but the thought keeps coming back, and then I can’t really settle until I check.
Do these nagging thoughts or the need to check things ever cause you to avoid certain situations or tasks because you know they’ll trigger the anxiety or checking urges?

Yes, somewhat. I wouldn’t say I avoid big things, but I do put things off because I know I’ll get stuck checking. Unpacking the condo has taken much longer than it really should, because I keep feeling like I need to verify where things are or whether I’ve misplaced something.

And I’ve been delaying my library tutoring preparation and some hobbies, too. It’s like I feel I can’t move on to those until I’m sure enough about the other things.
Do you ever try to resist or ignore the nagging thoughts, or do they feel like something you fully believe in and can’t easily question?

I do try to talk myself out of them, yes. I’ll tell myself, “That’s probably not true,” or “It’s unlikely I threw that away,” but the thought doesn’t really go away. It comes back, and then I start feeling unsettled until I check or at least think through it again. So I don’t fully believe it, but it’s hard to ignore.
